messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Chukwu's Unraveling

Chukwu was twenty-three when a routine traffic stop became the event that would hollow him out from the inside. He had been driving home from an assignment in East Baltimore, where he'd been gathering interviews for a piece on community policing. The officer who pulled him over said it was a broken taillight. Chukwu remembered the flashlight beam cutting through the driver's-side window, the command to keep his hands visible, the way the officer's partner positioned himself at the rear passenger door. What he remembered most vividly—what lived in his body now, two years later—was the moment the first officer's hand moved toward his belt, the sharp intake of breath, the metallic *click* of a gun being drawn. There had been shouting. Chukwu's hands had been shaking so badly he could barely grip the steering wheel. The officers had eventually realized their mistake—a case of mistaken identity, a car matching a description from a robbery three counties over—but by then the damage was done. They had kept their weapons drawn for what felt like an eternity, and Chukwu had spent those seconds certain he was going to die.

Now, at twenty-five, Chukwu existed in a state of perpetual vigilance that had begun to consume his life. When he heard footsteps behind him on the street—the sound of someone's shoes on pavement, the pace quickening or slowing—his entire nervous system would ignite. His chest would tighten, his breath would shallow, and he would feel the old terror flood through him as if the traffic stop were happening again. That auditory trigger would pull him immediately into a state of heightened threat detection: he would begin checking behind him compulsively, scanning for danger, unable to assess whether an unfamiliar street or a crowded market posed actual risk or merely the possibility of it. These moments of acute threat detection had taught him a hard lesson: the only way to avoid that spiral was to avoid the places where footsteps might find him. He had stopped taking the direct route to the corner store, stopped accepting invitations to venues he didn't know, stopped allowing himself anywhere unfamiliar—each avoidance a small bargain he made with his nervous system to keep the panic at bay. Living in that constant state of threat, he had begun to perceive danger in almost anything—the way a stranger's hand moved in a pocket, the angle at which a car was parked, even the particular quality of silence before someone spoke—each detail feeding his conviction that the world remained as lethal as the moment the officer's hand had moved toward his belt. When the world felt this dangerous, staying small and invisible seemed like the only strategy that made sense. He wore the dark clothes not as fashion but as camouflage; he avoided the newsroom not out of laziness but because a crowded space full of strangers felt like a minefield waiting to detonate. The threat was everywhere, and so the only rational response was to shrink the space in which he moved. Because he could no longer trust his own judgment about safety, he had started avoiding unfamiliar places altogether. The footsteps also yanked up the memory itself—vivid, intrusive, more real than the present moment—and with it came the crushing weight of his negative appraisals: the certainty that he was no longer the person he had been, that his life had been fundamentally destroyed, that he had lost the capacity to do the work that had once defined him.

The memories themselves had become almost unbearable. When Chukwu tried to recall the event—to explain it to his partner, to a therapist, to anyone—the narrative would fracture. He would start to describe the officer's voice and suddenly lose the thread entirely, unable to articulate what had happened or why it mattered so much. The memories were accompanied by auditory flashbacks: he would hear the officer's shout, the crackle of the radio, the sound of the gun's hammer being drawn, replaying in his mind with such intensity that he sometimes couldn't distinguish between what was happening now and what had happened then. Once these vivid recollections surfaced, they seemed to generate new threats everywhere: the sound of a car door slamming became indistinguishable from the memory of the gun being drawn, and the sight of a uniform in a crowd would send him searching backward through time, unable to stay present. The conviction that he was fundamentally broken, that something essential had been destroyed in him, seemed to pull these memories back again and again—as if he needed to return to that moment to find the exact point where he had been lost, to confirm that the damage was real and irreversible. If he was no longer the person he had been, then the things he used to do—the newsroom, the interviews, the music, the intimacy with his partner—were no longer available to him. So he had stopped trying. The dark, oversized clothing, the withdrawal from work and from her touch, the way he had learned to numb himself to anything that carried emotional weight—these were not choices so much as the only logical response to a life he believed was fundamentally destroyed. These vivid, intrusive recollections reinforced his conviction that something fundamental had broken in him—that he had become someone incapable of resilience, someone for whom the ordinary world had become a minefield. He found himself thinking, with a kind of hopeless certainty, that he used to be happy, that he used to be able to move through the world without fear, that the person he had been before the traffic stop no longer existed.

This belief—that he was destroyed, that he could no longer do the things that had once made him who he was—had begun to drive his behavior in ways that only deepened the trap. Because he believed his life was ruined and that he was no longer capable, Chukwu had started wearing dark, oversized clothing to make himself less visible, less noticeable. He had begun avoiding anything that might trigger grief or sadness—which meant avoiding his partner's attempts at intimacy, avoiding the newsroom where he used to feel alive, avoiding even the music that had once sustained him. When certain songs came on the radio, songs that had played during happier moments or that simply carried emotional weight, he would feel the panic rising again, the sense that feeling anything—joy or sorrow—was dangerous. So he had learned to shut it all down. He had become, in his own mind, a person who could not afford to feel. Yet this avoidance only confirmed what he already believed: that he was no longer capable of the things that had defined him. His editor had begun asking questions about his absences. His partner had grown quiet, hurt by his withdrawal. The more he avoided, the more isolated he became, and the more isolated he became, the more the threat felt real and omnipresent. Every unfamiliar street corner seemed to hold danger. Every set of footsteps behind him felt like a prelude to violence.

Chukwu had come to therapy because his partner had finally said, in a voice thick with concern and exhaustion, that she was losing him. He sat in the office now, a tall man made smaller by the weight he was carrying, and acknowledged that he didn't know how to live like this anymore. What frightened him most was not just the memory of the traffic stop itself, but the person he had become in response to it—someone afraid of his own shadow, someone who had learned to disappear into concealment and numbness. He wanted to know if it was possible to become himself again, or if the man he had been before that night was truly gone forever.
